 FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop; no indication of 'nefarious attack' 
 Homeland Security said there is no indication yet this was a "nefarious" act. 
 Live In this Sept. 25, 2025, file photo, Chicago O'Hare (ORD) International Airport is shown. Adobe Stock By Ayesha Ali and Ivan Pereira November 13, 2026, 5:14 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop Friday for all airports due to a communication issue affecting air traffic control.
 The agency's alert said the stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
 In this Oct. 20, 2015, file photo, the Air Traffic Control Tower and Terminal 4 at JFK Airport is shown in New York. Adobe Stock Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters Friday evening that the federal government is investigating, there was no indication yet that the incident was a "nefarious attack" and that everyone is safe.
 "It's just a telecommunications outage as of now," he told reporters.
 Mullin said the government will look into the root of the problem.
 "This isn't another 9/11. I cannot repeat that enough," he added.
 Shortly after the stop was issued, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an X statement that it was "due a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."
 "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in an X post.
 This is the second time since Sept. 11, 2001, that the FAA has ordered a nationwide ground stop. The last time was in 2023 , when the FAA NOTAM system went down and pilots could not get their pre-departure paperwork.
 In this 2018, file photo, the Miami International Airport is shown. Adobe Stock Air Route Traffic Control Centers are responsible for all flights above 18,000 feet. There are 22 of those centers in the U.S.
 Pilots who are in the air have flight plans and are prepared to continue with their flight path in case of such an emergency, according to ABC News contributor John Nance.

 "All pilots in that environment know what to do," Nance told ABC News on Friday.
 "It is a matter of predictability. Air Traffic Control knows that airplane is going to come out of the sky at some point of time looking for a pathway," he later added.
 Earlier in the afternoon, the FAA issued a ground stop at both Chicago's O'Hare and Midway airports due to equipment outage.
